claims.text: As-cast HfMoTaTiZr has a density of 10.21 g/cm³.
As-cast HfMoTaTiZr has a room-temperature yield strength of approximately 1600 MPa.
As-cast HfMoTaTiZr has a yield strength of approximately 855 MPa at 1000 °C.
As-cast HfMoTaTiZr has good ductility.
Replacing part of Hf with lower-atomic-weight Sc will reduce the density of HfMoTaTiZr.
Sc substitution can reduce density by more than 5–10%, reaching below 10 g/cm³.
Sc-modified HfMoTaTiZr can retain room- and high-temperature mechanical performance within 95% of the as-cast baseline.
The tested compositions will be Hf1−xScxMoTaTiZr with x = 0.05 and 0.10.
The modified alloys will be made by the same as-cast route, without homogenization or thermomechanical processing.
Sc substitution is expected to preserve a homogeneous single-phase microstructure.
The original HfMoTaTiZr alloy has a homogeneous single-phase microstructure.
A homogeneous solid-solution microstructure can provide strengthening in refractory high-entropy alloys.
Hf produces strong solution hardening in a refractory alloy.
Sc substitution will retain the lattice distortion and strengthening effects otherwise provided by Hf.
The refractory character of Sc will preserve phase stability in HfMoTaTiZr.
Preserved phase stability and dislocation-mediated deformation will maintain room- and high-temperature yield strength.
The modified alloy will have a room-temperature yield strength of approximately 1520–1600 MPa.
The modified alloy will have a yield strength of approximately 810–855 MPa at 1000 °C.
Sc substitution will limit the ductility loss to less than 10–15% relative to the baseline.
Density, yield strength, elongation, phase composition, and microstructural homogeneity will be measured for x = 0, 0.05, and 0.10 under quasi-static tensile loading at room temperature and 1000 °C.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis requires strength within 95% of baseline, allowing at most a 5% loss, whereas the rejection rule permits losses of up to 10%.

A density merely below 10 g/cm³ represents only slightly more than a 2% reduction from 10.21 g/cm³ and therefore does not necessarily meet the separately stated target of a greater than 5–10% reduction.
The text describes x = 0.05 and 0.10 in Hf1−xScxMoTaTiZr as 5–10 at.% substitution, but normalization of those formulas gives only 1 and 2 at.% Sc in the complete five-component alloy.

The hypothesis only requires that a suitable partial-substitution level exist, but the rule says failure of any substituted alloy falsifies the hypothesis, even if another tested substitution level succeeds.
